title: My palm is small
hookLine: Rumi: the eye of the senses is like a palm on the elephant, touching only part (Masnavi 3.1259ff)

cards: Two people describe the same family dinner. One says it was lovely. The other says it was a disaster.
They were at the same table. Two coworkers describe the same boss: one sees a tough mentor, the other a bully. Most arguments aren't between someone who's right and someone who's wrong.
They're between people each holding a real piece of something too big to hold whole. Rumi told a story about that, one you may have heard in another form.
In his version, it's very dark, and there's an elephant in the room.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT IN A DARK HOUSE.
teach.b: It's in Book Three of the Masnavi. Some travelers from India bring an elephant to a town where no one has ever seen one. They keep it in a dark house.
Crowds come, but it's pitch black inside, so everyone has to feel it with their hands. One person's hand lands on the trunk.

teach.h: A PIPE, A FAN, A PILLAR, A THRONE.
teach.b: It's like a water pipe, he says. Another touches the ear: it's like a fan. Another finds a leg: no, it's a pillar.
Another lays a hand on its back: it's like a throne. Each of them is describing something real. None of them is lying.
And every one of them is wrong about the elephant. Then Rumi gives the key.

teach.h: THE PALM CAN'T REACH IT ALL.
teach.b: The eye of the senses, he says, is only like the palm of the hand, and the palm can't reach all of the elephant. If each of them had carried a candle, their differences would have disappeared. The story is old.
A version with blind men and an elephant appears much earlier in a Buddhist text called the Udana, and a Persian poet before Rumi, Sanai, told it too. Rumi's point is about how we know.
Our senses, our opinions, our clever arguments are palms in the dark.
They touch real things, but they're small, and the elephant is very large. So Rumi's candle isn't a better hand. It's a different kind of seeing, what Sufis call the eye of the heart.
Before you insist it's a pillar, it's worth remembering where your hand is. Your line: remembering where your hand is.

how: The elephant story is told in several traditions; readers of Rumi usually take his version as a teaching on the limits of the senses and the need for the eye of the heart.

o: a whole too big for any one hand to touch
a big problem everyone pretends not to see
a memory that never fades or slips away

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: in Rumi's version, the people touching the elephant are blind
in his telling they can see; it's the house that's dark.
a version of the story appears in an earlier Buddhist text
the Udana tells it with blind men; the Persian poet Sanai told it before Rumi too.
Rumi says a candle would have ended their differences
if each had carried a candle, he says, the differences would have gone.

games.q: you're in the dark house, your hand on something long and round. everyone around you is arguing. what does Rumi say would settle it?
games.why: with a candle in each hand, Rumi says, their differences would have disappeared.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you're sure about, a person, a disagreement, a situation at home or work, and feel your hand on your piece of it.
Then ask gently what someone at the other end might be touching, and what you'd see with a candle. You don't have to change your mind; just remember the size of the elephant.

wordCard.voice: Elephant. Rumi's image for a hidden whole: each hand in the dark touches something real, but none touches all of the elephant. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: an elephant. Rumi's section is titled the elephant in the dark house.

carryVoice: Your line: remembering where your hand is. Every palm touches something real, and none holds it all. See you tomorrow.
